#8417. Andrew Skurka on Vapor Barrier Liners for Winter Camping

This article is adapted from Andrew Skurka’s first-person video for The Trek’s YouTube channel, part of a weekly series. Edited for clarity and readability.

On a multi-day winter backpacking trip, your own sweat can become one of your biggest problems. Moisture builds up in your gloves, boots, insulated jackets, and sleeping bag. When temperatures stay below freezing, drying everything out can be nearly impossible.

That’s where vapor barrier liners (VBLs) come in. These intentionally non-breathable layers keep perspiration from reaching your insulation. They can feel clammy and take some getting used to, but in the right conditions they can make a remarkable difference.

I learned this the hard way. I was the first person to complete the Sea-to-Sea Route, and during that trip I spent the winter on the trail, snowshoeing 1,400 miles through Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. In January 2007, a few months before the Great Western Loop, I hiked about 380 miles along Minnesota’s North Shore from Duluth to Ely, a trip I called Ultralight in the Nation’s Icebox. And I started the Alaska-Yukon Expedition in mid-March in Kotzebue, north of the Arctic Circle. I still remember that for the first three days, the temperature never got above 15 degrees below zero.

The Sea-to-Sea Route was my first legitimate winter backpacking experience, and I wore a pretty traditional layering system. It was basically an extension of what I’d wear in three-season conditions:

When I say cold, I mean daytime temperatures that never get above freezing, ideally no warmer than the 20s, and nighttime lows in the single digits or teens. The same problem applies at anything colder.

You’re active during the day. In the heat of the day, when it’s 20 degrees out and you’re really moving on snowshoes or skis, you might wear just a midweight base layer, or maybe you need a fleece. Either way, you’re perspiring from the activity. And at night, your body is still losing moisture through insensible perspiration.

If you’re wearing all of your layers at night inside a sleeping bag, that moisture moves out through your layering system. It usually gets trapped in my active insulated jacket, or on the inside of my waterproof-breathable shell, or, if I’m in my sleeping bag, inside my big arctic puffy. As the moisture moves away from your body, it gets colder and colder until it hits the dew point, and that point is often inside your layering system or inside your sleeping bag.

Even if you’ve never backpacked in winter, this has probably happened to you. After a day of alpine skiing at a resort, you notice the inside of your gloves is pretty wet. So is the inside of your plastic ski boots.

That’s not a problem if you’re out for the day, because you get home or into a hut and dry everything out. On a backpacking trip, you can’t. You can’t dry out your sleeping bag, your boots, your gloves, or your big belay parka, so the moisture stays trapped. All your stuff gets wet and stays wet, and when it’s wet, it’s also cold.

That was my failing on the Sea-to-Sea Route back in 2004 and 2005. I could go out for a night or two, but by nights three, four, and five, moisture was accumulating in my layers and my sleeping bag. After a couple of days out, I needed to get inside somewhere warm and dry so I could reset all of my systems and safely go out again.

A vapor barrier liner is a non-breathable layer worn just outside a thin or midweight base layer and underneath your insulating layers. The fluorescent orange jacket I’m wearing in the video is an example. Instead of allowing perspiration to move into your fleece, parka, or sleeping bag, the barrier keeps that moisture closer to your skin.

There’s a tradeoff: the sweat doesn’t magically disappear. It stays inside the barrier, where your base layer may become damp or clammy. That’s why I pay close attention to how hard I’m working, and I vent or adjust layers before I start sweating heavily.

If you’re considering multi-day backpacking or thru-hiking in winter with daytime temperatures consistently around 20°F or colder, I think vapor barrier liners are well worth looking into. They can significantly reduce the moisture buildup I just described, although they don’t replace good temperature management or protection from outside moisture.

With vapor barrier liners, your layering system looks like this:

For more on building a clothing system from a small set of versatile pieces, see The Only 12 Backpacking Clothes You Really Need.

The first benefit is that a vapor barrier liner protects your exterior layers. It keeps them warm by keeping them dry.

With the VBL on, I’m still perspiring a little, but much of that body moisture is stopped by the barrier instead of moving into my fleece or insulated parkas. At night, I can wear my insulating layers inside my sleeping bag while greatly reducing how much perspiration reaches the bag’s insulation. It won’t make my sleeping bag waterproof or eliminate every source of condensation, but it helps protect against moisture coming from my body.

If you’re wearing what’s almost a trash bag next to your skin, you’re going to be very aware of how much you’re perspiring, because it starts to feel clammy. When you feel that clamminess, it’s your sign to moderate your effort, so maybe you go slower, or to start taking layers off.

Sometimes you’re in between. You don’t want to take a layer off because you’re not that warm, but you definitely need to expel some heat and moisture. That’s when you ventilate. RBH Designs makes a fantastic vapor barrier outer layer, like the one I’m wearing, with all sorts of venting features: a full front zip, pit zips, and zippers on the arms. You can keep wearing the layer but really open it up so the heat and moisture escape.

In very cold weather, you don’t want a lot of ways to lose heat, which is why you carry lots of puffy layers and multiple layers. Without a vapor barrier liner, moisture moves through your layers, and as it gets close to the outside, it evaporates. That evaporation steals heat away from you. A VBL does an excellent job of keeping your heat next to you and preventing that evaporative heat loss.

Here’s a classic scenario that even three-season backpackers will relate to. You hike up a mountain without moderating your effort much. As you climb, it gets cooler and cooler, maybe you enter the clouds and lose the sun, and when you finally reach the top, your back is drenched and your hair is wet with sweat. Then, as you’re signing the summit register, you start getting cold, because all that sweat is evaporating off your body. A vapor barrier liner keeps that moisture inside. You can think of it as its own microclimate, so you don’t get that evaporative heat loss.

If you want to wander into vapor barrier liners, start with gloves. My layering system for really cold weather starts with the DeFeet Duraglove wool glove. It’s definitely a liner glove, but it has more heft than most. Over that, I go straight to the RBH Designs mitts.

When I notice my hands starting to get clammy from sweat, it’s easy. I take the mitt off and loop it onto a carabiner on my backpack’s shoulder strap. Then I can ski or snowshoe for a while without it, and when my hand starts to get cold again, I put the mitt back on.

Again, the idea with vapor barrier liners is that you become sensitive to your rate of perspiration, and you either moderate your effort or take off or adjust layers so that you sweat less.

With daytime temperatures no warmer than the teens, I would move toward vapor barrier liner socks. Here’s how the system works, from the inside out:

Then all of that goes into my boot. For those curious, mine are old-school leather three-pin telemark boots, where the telemark binding clamps down on the duckbill at the front.

Vapor barrier liner socks become important because otherwise the sweat from your feet gets into the outer layers of the boot, or gets trapped inside it, and then it’s tough to get the boot dry.

The very last thing you’d add to your vapor barrier liner system is a pair of vapor barrier liner pants. It has to be pretty cold to warrant them, with daytime highs in the low to mid teens and ideally in the single digits. Your legs generate so much heat that it has to be really cold before you’d want running tights with vapor barrier liner pants on top.

As with the top, you want the pants to be really well ventilated, maybe with full or three-quarter zips on the legs. That way you can easily open them up to let the heat and moisture out, and keep moving without having to take the pants off completely because you’re overheating and sweating too much.

With all the temperature ranges I’ve given you, keep in mind that they depend on the other conditions: how much sun there is, how much wind there is, and whether you’re walking on dirt, which absorbs a lot more solar radiation, or on ice or snow, which reflects the sun back at you. You might adjust these recommendations up or down for when to start using vapor barrier liners.

Vapor barrier clothing is a niche category, so you won’t find many options in mainstream backpacking stores. Rab makes vapor barrier socks, and Western Mountaineering offers a vapor barrier liner for sleeping bags.

For purpose-built VBL clothing, I recommend looking at RBH Designs. I’ve had excellent experiences with its equipment, including vapor barrier mitts, socks, and ventilated jackets. As with any specialized winter gear, check current availability and sizing before purchasing.

In addition to jackets, pants, socks, and mitts, there’s another commercially available option: a vapor barrier liner for your sleeping bag. You wear your base layer shirt, pants, and socks, then sleep inside the VBL, which goes inside your sleeping bag.

That’s an effective way to reduce perspiration getting into your sleeping bag’s down or synthetic insulation, because most of the body moisture stays inside the liner’s microclimate. It won’t, however, protect your sleeping bag from moisture coming from outside the liner.

My big hang-up with a vapor barrier sleeping bag liner is that you can’t use it during the day. You still end up with the same situation: you have on your liner gloves and a normal mountaineering mitt, your hands are sweating, and that sweat is making its way into the insulation of the mitt. That’s not going to help you on day two. I think it’s better to have vapor barrier liner technology not only at night, to keep your sleeping bag from getting wet, but also during the day, to keep your outer layers from getting wet.

What’s the minimum trip length where I’d want vapor barrier liners? My answer is anything of one night or more.

Suppose it’s a two-day, one-night trip, and it’s two full days. If you follow the conventional wisdom of using breathable layers, you have your liner gloves and a standard overmitt without a vapor barrier liner. At the end of the first day, your mitt is very wet and very cold. When you wake up in the morning and put it back on, it’s not going to be as nice to wear as it was on the first day.

With boots, you’re perspiring through your feet all day long, and that moisture gets trapped inside your boot. When you wake up in the morning, your boot is going to be frozen. I’ve done a lot of very uncomfortable things in the outdoors, but one of the most uncomfortable is putting your foot inside a frozen boot.

If you ever end up with wet shoes, either from your sweat or from external water like a creek crossing, the key is what you do when you pull into camp at night. Open up the shoe, really extend the tongue, and loosen the laces as much as you possibly can. Then just let it freeze overnight. In the morning, jam your feet inside, and the warmth of your feet will sort of thaw it out. If it freezes in that open position, you can at least get your feet into the shoe.

One additional advantage of using vapor barrier liners is that I can rely more confidently on down insulation during long winter trips. You don’t need VBLs to use down in winter, but limiting the body moisture that reaches it helps preserve its warmth over consecutive days.

You’ve probably heard the usual pros and cons of down versus synthetic insulation. Down generally offers more warmth for its weight. And while synthetic insulation tends to retain more warmth than down when damp, the idea that it stays fully warm when wet is misleading. Wet synthetic insulation still loses insulating performance, just usually not as much as wet down.

With a vapor barrier protecting my outer layers from perspiration, I can use a down sleeping bag, a down belay parka, and even a down active parka with less concern about that particular source of moisture. Those pieces are generally excellent for warmth-to-weight, and good down insulation can last for many years. My GoLite down belay parka dates back to 2009. A VBL doesn’t protect any of this gear from snow, rain, or other outside moisture, though, so keeping it dry still matters.

I’ve been talking about vapor barrier liners for a long time. I used them extremely successfully on Ultralight in the Nation’s Icebox in 2007 and the Alaska-Yukon Expedition in 2010. Yet in the last 15 or 20 years, the market hasn’t changed very much. There are a few good products out there, but the selection is still small.

That’s fine. I think there’s a very small market for vapor barrier liners because, let’s be honest, not many people go out in the wintertime on multi-day or multi-night trips. The days are short, the nights are long, it’s very cold, and it can be kind of lonely.

But winter can also be a beautiful time to be in the backcountry. It extends your season if you want to do more than backpack between June and September. It’s a way to expand your skill set, and you may learn things you can apply to your three-season trips. Getting out at all times of the year, not just when the weather’s nice, will definitely make you a better backpacker.

There’s not a lot of information out there about vapor barrier liners. I wrote a blog post about them years ago that now has more than 200 comments. If you have questions about vapor barrier liners, ask them in the comments on the video, and I’ll try to get to them.

On multi-day winter trips, body moisture can build up in your layers and sleeping bag night after night, and drying everything out may be impossible. A vapor barrier liner worn just outside your base layer reduces how much perspiration reaches your insulation, makes you more aware of when you’re sweating, and helps limit evaporative heat loss. I consider VBLs especially worthwhile when daytime temperatures stay around 20°F or colder: start with mitts, consider socks when highs are in the teens, and save pants for particularly cold conditions. Even for a single overnight trip in those conditions, they’re worth a serious look. You still need to manage your sweat and keep outside moisture off your gear.

Andrew Skurka has backpacked more than 30,000 miles and has been named Adventurer of the Year by both Outside and National Geographic. He is the author of The Ultimate Hiker’s Gear Guide and founded his guided backpacking program in 2011.

Skurka no longer guides winter trips, but his team leads guided backpacking trips in three-season conditions in southern Utah, the High Sierra, Alaska, and Yellowstone. The 2027 schedule will be posted by November 6, 2026, and applications open December 7, 2026.

#8415. A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8414. Feds Unveil Plan to Overhaul National Wildlife Refuges, Get More ‘Boots on the Ground’

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:06 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Following a 6-month review of the operation, purpose, and function of America’s National Wildlife Refuges, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service today announced an initiative to improve habitat, expand refuge access, and redirect resources to field operations.

Results of the internal refuge review were greeted with relief by wildlife organizations, some of which worried that the Trump administration intended to divest some refuges or to weaken their role as America’s top-tier wildlife properties.

In comments this morning at the Audubon NWR in North Dakota, both Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and USFWS Director Brian Nesvik outlined 29 recommendations that generally support refuge field operations, improve both public access and administrative efficiency, and boost law enforcement resources.

However, with a 20 percent cut in funding and the loss of nearly a third of its workforce, it’s unclear how the Service will implement some of today’s directives.

The recommendations announced today are compiled in a program called Rooted In Purpose that generally increases the Department of Interior’s investments in the National Wildlife Refuge System that includes 573 refuges across 95 million acres of land. Nesvik announced the initiative in December 2025 and tapped fellow Wyomingite and senior advisor Joshua Coursey to conduct the 6-month review. Nesvik further detailed the background and sideboards of the refuge review in a wide-ranging interview with Outdoor Life in January 2026.

“Our purpose is simply to confirm that [each] refuges’ original purpose still aligns with the Service’s current mission,” Nesvik told Outdoor Life in January. “People have assumed that means we’re looking for ways to sell land. That is not the intent. The intent is to make sure we’re still doing those things that were intended when the refuge was created but also to make sure that things aren’t completely askew from our current mission.”

Today’s announcement, which is also detailed in a Secretarial Order entitled “Making America’s National Wildlife Refuges Great Again” issued by Burgum, distilled the 6-month review into four main areas of focus that the Service will apply over the next two years.

Nesvik noted today that his Director’s Order 230 resulted in 41 in-person refuge visits, 118 virtual visits, and four regional office visits along with internal surveys that solicited more than 1,000 responses from USFWS staff, and an external survey that received more than 2,000 responses.

“Refuge employees know what the land needs and what it takes to get the work done,” Nesvik said today in remarks delivered at the North Dakota refuge. “Their experience shaped this review, and their input will help us put its recommendations into action. We are focused on giving them practical tools and clear guidance to manage habitat, protect wildlife and provide Americans with quality hunting, fishing and other outdoor opportunities.”

Today’s news was generally welcomed by wildlife organizations.

“The USFWS refuge system has been an important part of the conservation successes in North America,” said Corey Mason, CEO and executive vice president of conservation for the Wild Sheep Foundation. “We applaud Secretary Burgum and Director Nesvik’s efforts to refocus the refuge system on the field work necessary to ensure quality habitat for wildlife and opportunity for Americans to benefit from that work and access these unique places.”

Ariel Weigard, vice president for government affairs for Pheasants Forever and Quail Forever commended Burgum and Nesvik “for their efforts to strengthen the National Wildlife Refuge System and its ability to deliver conservation on the ground.”

Today’s announcement didn’t detail how the Rooted in Purpose initiative will be funded and implemented. The USFWS budget has been cut by about 20 percent, or some $323 million in the Trump administration’s 2027 budget. Programs that have been either cut or eliminated next year include state and tribal wildlife grants, migratory bird conservation funds, and the entire National Wildlife Refuge Fund.

The Rooted in Purpose program provides some insights in how funding might be redirected to achieve the goals of refuge reform. The document details the Service intends to eliminate the Urban Wildlife Conservation Program Policy and “redirect all discretionary program funding to activities that directly support the conservation mission.”

The directive also prioritizes what it calls “boots on the ground.”

Read Next: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Land Is Worse Than You Thought

“Reduce headquarters and regional office staffing and reallocate positions to refuge operations, prioritizing the people needed to manage habitat, maintain facilities, support public access and protect resources.”

Lastly, the Service intends to stretch limited resources by using “technology and Super Intelligence to improve efficiency” and to promote contracting and reducing barriers for “for qualified local businesses competing for federal work.”

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8411. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

The icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein

The icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

The skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

#8410. The Best Gifts for Hunters: Get Them What They Actually Want

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:22 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Hunters can present a challenge when it comes to gift buying. They already have one of these or two of those. They don’t particularly care for Model A or Brand B. There’s always the $100 Gift Card, but you really don’t want to be that impersonal, now do you?

Fortunately, there’s an almost endless array of “I’d love one of those” gift ideas whether the hunter on your list chases waterfowl, big game, upland birds, or small game. This year, the following gift ideas will help you put the right hunting gear beneath the tree.

Missing a target means lost or broken arrows. Not only does that get expensive, it’s downright discouraging. The BlackOut LongShot 36 is a big target that allows bowhunters to confidently practice shooting their bows at extended ranges without worrying about missing the target. Best of all, it’s affordable. In my testing, I’ve found arrow removal is easy, even though I’m shooting small-diameter arrows over 290 fps.

Even if you’re shopping for a bowhunter who already owns a backyard target, they’ll still want and need this one. It’s a can’t-miss gift for anyone who loves flinging arrows.

Thermal monoculars are handy devices to have around the house and in the field. They can help you locate coyotes in the pitch dark, blood trail a deer (where legal) and make home repairs, such as finding heat leaking out of a window. The key to choosing a thermal as a gift is understanding that the more you spend, the better the image gets. But not all use cases require top-end performance. If someone is going to use their thermal to scan fields, recover game, and use around the property, a lower-resolution sensor works well. If they need to view and identify animals at longer ranges (beyond 100 yards), they’ll need a top-of-the-line unit.

The ATN BlazeSeeker 6 is a compact thermal that slips easily into a pocket and can record photos and videos. It costs only $429 to $489 and is ideal for everyday use around the property and in the field. If you’re buying for someone who needs more capability, I recommend the BlazeTrek 6. The BlazeTrek 6 has a better image and costs $795 to $1,499. Both monoculars are easy to use, and the ATN app has a handy AI assistant to guide you through any snags the recipient might encounter. Any hunter will be thrilled to receive an ATN monocular, and it’s another fantastic gift to consider.

Good gifts are practical, but the best gifts help people have fun. One of the keys to having fun in the outdoors is being comfortable no matter the conditions. The Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket is a highly versatile, packable layer that’s ideal for staying outside when the weather turns cold. From fishing to late-season hunting, this is an outer shell that will get a ton of use. We’ve tested and recommended the Foundry Jacket. You can read our full review to learn more.

Soft cases are the practical way to carry a shotgun to the range or to your hunting spot. They’re something that every bird hunter needs and will use regularly. They’re also relatively affordable, which makes them a great gift. The Evolution Outdoor Rawhide Classic Camo Shotgun Case is a stylish and practical case that’s made from waxed canvas. It will carry shotguns up to 50 inches in overall length, so it will accommodate most semi-automatics with 28-inch or shorter barrels and double guns with up to 30-inch barrels.

It’s tough buying the right knife for an outdoorsman, but you can’t go wrong with the iconic Victorinox Huntsman made by the folks who produced the original Swiss Army Knife™. The Huntsman has 15 functions, including blades, corkscrew, reamer, punch and sewing awl, scissors, wood saw, wire stripper, screwdrivers, and more. It’s available in 7 different color patterns. You can be sure that the outdoorsman on your list will find unlimited uses for this versatile Swiss-made tool through the many seasons that it will serve them.

Built to handle rough roads, bad weather, and air travel, this is a gift that tells someone you understand their passion and want to protect the tools that make it possible. It’s designed to hold two scoped rifles, with thick protective foam inside and six sturdy latches that keep everything sealed tight. Whether you’re shopping for a hunter that drives to the deer camp or flies out west for elk season, this case gives them peace of mind that their firearms will arrive zeroed and ready to hunt.— Scott Einsmann

You can get a turkey hunter a new call, a knife, or this piece of turkey hunting culture. The Tenth Legion is a book that captures the heart of what it is to be a diehard turkey hunter and is guaranteed to be enjoyed by anyone that chases gobbles throughout the spring. It was written by the legendary Colonel Tom Kelly, who recently passed on. I keep a copy of the Tenth Legion in my vest and read through it when the birds aren’t feeling talkative, and I highly recommend it as a gift for the turkey obsessed. — Scott Einsmann

Securely packaging your hard-won wild game, be it fresh venison, wild turkey, or mallard duck breasts has never been as easy as it is now, thanks to Cabela’s Deluxe 12 (D12) vacuum sealer. Weighing just four pounds, the D12 features a heavy-duty commercial vacuum pump designed for years of service. User-friendly, easy-to-clean, and programmable, the D12 takes up little counter space, while offering multiple modes of operation including manual seal, pulse, Auto/Vac, Standard, and Extended, as well as ‘Canister’ option great for preserving tough-to-seal foodstuffs.

This chest pack is designed to hold a hunter’s binoculars, and much much more. For backcountry hunters, a chest pack is a critical piece of gear and there are few out there that offer more features than the Kuiu Pro. It includes: magnetic closure for maximum quietness, adjustable main pouch for proper bino fit, rail-lock system for bottom accessory, rail-lock mount for ammo holder, plus a variety of extra pockets. It comes in five different camo/solid color options (I don’t think you can go wrong with solid Ash). This is an ideal gift for a big game hunter or even a turkey hunter, who needs quick access to optics and other critical gear.

A cellular trail camera is a perfect gift for any deer or turkey hunter. If the hunter already has a cell cam, they’ll be happy to have another (you can never have too many cameras out there). And if they don’t have camera yet, then your gift will get them in the game. And there’s not a trail camera out there that’s more effective and easy to use than the Tactacam 4.0. The Outdoor Life crew thoroughly tests trail cams every year, and the Tactacam 4.0 won the editor’s choice award, hands down, in 2026. Features include: Up to 4K photo definition, up to 96 feet of flash range, Low-glow or no-glow flash settings, 16 gb of internal storage, powered by 12 AA batteries, live video, on-demand photos, GPS enabled.

Sure, the description says ‘Waterfowl Backpack,’ and all duck hunters should have one of these, but don’t let the name fool you. This well-built large capacity pack has 101 uses in the field, e.g. camera bag, lunch box, blind bag, and dry clothes storage to name just a handful. With over 1,550 cubic inches of interior space, the Northern Flight backpack is crafted of rugged 600D polyester with a water-resistant polyurethane coating to help keep what’s inside nice and dry. There’s plenty of pockets, glove-friendly zippers, a huge main compartment, hydration pouch, and MOLLE attachment points for additional capacity. In other words this is an excellent hunting pack for a variety of scenarios.

How many times have you wished for some warmth while waiting out that trophy whitetail from inside the chilly confines of that late January ground blind? Thanks to the innovative minds at TideWe and their heated hunting chair, turning up the thermostat just became possible. At first glance, the chair seems ordinary enough – adjustable height; swiveling through 360 degrees; armrests; and a detachable gear pouch. But this chair adds a little spice in the form of battery-powered heat. Three heat levels (100 through 130 degrees), long 10-hour  battery life at the lowest setting, and a fast three-hour charge time make this ‘hot seat’ a Must-Have this winter.

Hunters constantly need to keep knives and broadheads sharp. This folding field sharpener is a versatile and handy way to maintain everything from pocketknives to axes. It’s only $13, and I’ve been testing it while sharpening broadheads and honing knives. It works great, and I recommend it.

*I noticed this product has only a three-star rating from customer reviews. But the reviews are all for a fishing reel. This appears to be a glitch on the Bass Pro Shops/Cabela’s website.

There’s nothing worse than slipping your feet into cold wet boots. Fortunately, the folks at PEET Dryer have the answer in their original boot dryer. The PEET dryer uses convection to push warm air upwards through specially designed chambers and ports to dry shoes and boots of all shapes, sizes, and material types. Safe enough to operate 24/7, this makes the perfect gift for anyone who goes outside, but especially hunters who are prone to get their boots wet.

Hunters often like to forage while they’re in the field. But wild mushrooms are nothing to be guessed at when it comes to their edibility. Some make wonderful meals, while others can make a person terribly sick, or worse. This makes a good mushroom identification book an absolute necessity for the forestland forager. And few are as comprehensive as David Arora’s All That The Rain Promises, and More. An educator in the field of mycology, Arora’s easy to understand descriptive prose, along with his excellent photographs, takes much of the mystery out of separating the ‘good’ from the ‘not so good’ when it comes to fungi.

Virtually indestructible. That’s the best way to describe YETI’s latest introduction, the Loadout Gobox 1 Gear Case. Built out of what the company refers to as ‘Defender II Material,’ the Gobox 1 is the perfect hard case if you’re looking to safely store items such as a wallet, passport, keys, portable power, or anything else. The Gobox 1 seals out Mother Nature, while providing roughly 56 cubic inches of interior space, yet only weighing 1.7 pounds. The Gobox 1 is ideal for kayakers, rafting enthusiasts, off-roaders, mountain bikers, and of course, hunters. And it’s available in five different colors.

There are about 101 different ways to repel mosquitoes but few are as effective and easy to use as a ThermaCELL. The lightweight MR300 uses a cylindrical fuel canister to gently warm a small metal plate, which in turn activates the material infused into the unit’s repellent mat. This repellent diffuses into a 15 square-foot zone of protection around the unit, keeping mosquitoes at bay within 15 minutes and (under optimal conditions) for as long as four hours. No batteries. No DEET sprays. And it’s safe to use around pets.

Firearm maintenance should be a concern of all hunters. Fortunately, the Allen Company’s Breakthrough Clean Technologies Universal Cleaning Kit helps make the job much easier. Included in the tough ammo can container are a variety of nylon brushes, brass patch jags, two multi-section cleaning rods, patches, swabs, a silicone gun cloth, solvent, and a bottle of ‘Battle Born’ high purity gun oil. It’s everything you need to clean a gun in one place.

Even in these modern times of precision air rifles, there’s still something to be said about Old School stuff — like Crosman’s 760 Pumpmaster air rifle. Now here’s a tool developed specifically to introduce young or new shooters to the shooting sports. The 760 handles both .177 caliber pellets and BBs, sending them downrange at 615/700 and 645 feet-per-second, respectively. A crossbolt safety, synthetic stock/fore-end, grooved receiver to accommodate a 4x scope, and traditional front/rear blade sights make this the perfect gift for all ages.

#8408. Osprey ThrULite Pro 55L Review: Ultralight Comfort From a Backpacking Giant

Osprey is making a serious push into ultralight backpacking with the new ThrULite Pro series. Long known for its comfortable, feature-rich backpacks, the company is now targeting the ultralight market, long dominated by smaller manufacturers.

The ThrULite Pro comes in 20-, 40-, and 55-liter versions, with the 55L weighing just 1 pound, 11 ounces. That weight is competitive with packs from brands like Hyperlite Mountain Gear, Zpacks, and Gossamer Gear, yet the pack still retains some of the comfort-focused design Osprey is known for.

I tested the ThrULite Pro 55L throughout Maine during late summer and fall, putting in plenty of hiking and guiding miles on rocky trails and arduous mountain terrain. My regular pack is a Hyperlite Mountain Gear Southwest 55, so I was particularly interested in how Osprey’s new offering would compare.

After several months of use, the biggest surprise was just how comfortable this pack is. There are a few design choices I’d change, but Osprey has put together a compelling ultralight option that deserves a closer look.

MSRP: $340* Weight: 27 ounces | 765 grams Materials: “NanoFly” proprietary nylon/UHMWPE ripstop fabric Volume: 20L, 40L, 55L (I reviewed the 55L) Suspension: Minimalist frame with running vest-style harness Closure: Roll-top

I used the ThrULite Pro 55 on hiking and guiding trips throughout Maine in late summer and fall, including long days on rocky, root-covered trails and mountainous terrain. As a Registered Maine Guide, I regularly carry extra equipment for clients, making comfort and accessibility particularly important.

Conditions were mostly dry, with limited rain that provided some opportunity to evaluate the pack’s weather resistance.

One of the most notable features of the ThrULite Pro is its running vest-inspired shoulder harness, a departure from the traditional straps found on most backpacking packs. The design creates a close-fitting, body-hugging carry that distributes weight comfortably across the shoulders and upper body.

Combined with the minimalist suspension system, the result is a pack that feels remarkably comfortable despite weighing less than two pounds. Osprey has eliminated its familiar trampoline-style back panel, cutting weight while maintaining a supportive carrying system with a slimmer foam and mesh panel.

At just 27 ounces, the ThrULite Pro 55 is firmly in ultralight territory. Osprey uses a proprietary lightweight fabric and strips away unnecessary features, including the traditional top lid or “brain,” to keep weight down.

The pack instead uses a roll-top closure, a common feature among ultralight backpacks. While this reduces weight and simplifies the design, I found the closure a bit awkward to use. It also doesn’t allow the pack to cinch down and compress as tightly as I’d like, particularly when carrying smaller loads.

The ThrULite Pro maintains a relatively minimalist layout but offers plenty of exterior storage. The side water bottle pockets are tall and feature adjustable cinch closures at the top, allowing you to tighten them around bottles or other gear for a more secure hold. There’s also a large, deep rear pocket that provides generous storage for items you want to keep separate from the main compartment, such as a rain jacket or other frequently used gear.

The pack also includes two hipbelt pockets, one with a traditional zipper and the other with an elastic closure for quick access. Unfortunately, both are extremely small, limiting their usefulness for snacks, electronics, or other frequently accessed items. It’s an odd design choice considering how practical the rest of the exterior storage is.

Osprey’s proprietary fabric provides a reasonable degree of weather resistance without the weight of heavier traditional pack materials. During my limited rain testing, the fabric shed water effectively, with precipitation beading up and running off the surface.

That said, it didn’t appear to offer quite the same level of protection as Dyneema Composite Fabric (DCF), which is used in many ultralight packs. I didn’t experience prolonged or particularly heavy rain, so I can’t speak to how well the ThrULite Pro would hold up in sustained wet conditions. For longer trips, I’d still recommend using a pack liner to protect critical gear.

Comfort is easily the standout feature of the ThrULite Pro. After plenty of hiking and guiding miles, I found the pack extremely comfortable, with a stable, well-balanced carry that feels more substantial than its 27-ounce weight suggests.

The running vest-style harness and minimalist suspension work well together, providing a secure fit without the bulk of a traditional backpacking suspension system. Even over long days on Maine’s rugged trails, the pack remained comfortable and moved naturally with my body.

Coming from the Hyperlite Southwest 55, I was impressed by how well Osprey managed to combine low weight with the kind of carrying comfort the brand is known for.

Osprey has managed to bring a 55-liter pack below two pounds without making it feel overly stripped down. At 27 ounces, the ThrULite Pro compares favorably with many established ultralight packs.

The minimalist suspension, lightweight fabric, and lack of a traditional brain all contribute to the low weight. While there are lighter options available, the ThrULite Pro strikes a good balance between weight savings and comfort.

I’ve generally preferred minimalist backpacks, and the ThrULite Pro follows that approach. There aren’t a lot of unnecessary features or complicated adjustments, and the overall construction feels straightforward.

Osprey also brings the advantage of its established warranty and repair program, which could make the ThrULite Pro especially appealing to hikers considering their first ultralight pack.

My biggest complaint with the ThrULite Pro is the hipbelt pockets. Both are so small that they’re almost useless for practical storage.

I like having the option of a zippered pocket and an elastic closure, but neither provides enough room for much beyond the smallest essentials. When guiding or hiking long days, I frequently reach for snacks and other small items without stopping, so accessible hipbelt storage is particularly important.

Larger pockets would add minimal weight while making the pack considerably more functional. It’s a frustrating oversight on an otherwise well-designed backpack.

While I appreciate the weight savings from eliminating the traditional top lid, the roll-top system could use some refinement.

I found it somewhat awkward to close, and more importantly, it doesn’t allow the pack to compress as much as I’d like when carrying a smaller load. Compared with my HMG Southwest, which has a straightforward roll-top and side compression system, the Osprey feels less adaptable as gear volume changes.

It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s something I noticed regularly during testing.

The ThrULite Pro 55L is an impressive entry into the ultralight market from one of backpacking’s biggest manufacturers. At just 27 ounces, Osprey has created a pack that competes with established ultralight offerings while maintaining the comfort that has long been one of the company’s strengths.

After several months of hiking and guiding in Maine, carrying comfort was easily the highlight. The running vest-style harness and minimalist suspension provide an excellent fit, and the pack feels comfortable over long days on rugged terrain.

As previously mentioned, there are a few things I’d modify: the hipbelt pockets are frustratingly small, and the roll-top closure doesn’t compress as effectively as I’d like. I’d also want more time in sustained rain before making any definitive claims about its weather resistance.

Still, these are relatively minor drawbacks compared with how well the pack carries. For hikers looking to move into ultralight backpacking without giving up comfort, the ThrULite Pro 55L is well worth considering.

Hyperlite Mountain Gear Southwest 55 MSRP: $399 Weight: 29.3 oz (Size M) Capacity: 55L

Gossamer Gear Mariposa 60 MSRP: $315 Weight: 34.2 oz Capacity/Max Load: 60L / 35 lb

Zpacks Arc Haul Ultra 60L MSRP: $399 Weight: 22 oz Max Load: 40 lb

The Osprey ThrULite Pro 55 was donated for the purpose of review.

#8406. Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador.
